Article Title: Planning a trip to Canada: Immigration agency answers the visa questions travellers often get wrong
Article Text:
Canada’s immigration agency answered some common questions

How long will a visitor visa actually take?

What documents do you need?

Can you work or study while visiting?

Read IRCC complete post here

Millions of people visit Canada every year. Here are some of the top questions about visiting Canada, answered!

1. Do I need a visa or an electronic travel authorization (eTA) to travel to Canada?

To visit Canada, most people need a visitor visa or an electronic travel authorization (eTA), depending on their citizenship, their travel document and the way they plan to travel to Canada.

Check if you need a visa or an eTA.

2. How long does it take to get a visitor visa?

If you need a visitor visa, you must complete an application and provide the required documents, which may include documents proving your identity, travel plans and eligibility to enter Canada. Processing times vary, so check the latest estimated processing time before you apply.

3. What documents do I need to apply for a visitor visa?

Your application needs to include a digital copy of your passport or travel document, which should be valid (not expired) for at least 6 months from the date you plan to travel.

When you apply online, you’ll get a personalized document checklist in the portal. Make sure you provide all the required documents.

4. Can I work or study while visiting Canada?

Visitors cannot work or study in Canada unless they’re authorized to do so. If you want to work or study here, you may also need a work permit or study permit.

Canada’s immigration authority has stepped in to clear up some of the most common confusion facing travellers. IRCC shared a post of social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) publishing a set of answers to the questions it says that visitors ask most often and the responses are worth a read before you book that trip. With millions of people visiting Canada every year, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) says a handful of questions come up again and again. Here's what the agency wants every prospective visitor to know.This is where many travellers get caught out. If you do need a visitor visa, you'll have to submit an application along with supporting documents proving your identity, travel plans, and eligibility to enter Canada — and processing times can vary significantly depending on demand and your location. IRCC is urging applicants to check current estimated processing times before applying, rather than assuming last year's timeline still holds.At a minimum, your application needs a digital copy of your passport or travel document, and it must remain valid for at least six months beyond your planned travel date — a detail that trips up more travellers than you'd expect. The good news: applying online generates a personalised document checklist inside the portal, so you know exactly what's required for your specific case rather than guessing.Here's the one that catches people out the most. Visitors are not permitted to work or study in Canada unless they're specifically authorized to do so. If your trip involves any work or study plans, a standard visitor visa or eTA won't cut it — you'll likely need a separate work permit or study permit, and IRCC recommends checking eligibility for either well before you travel.
Article Summary: Millions of people visit Canada every year. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) says a handful of questions come up again and again. IRCC shared a post of social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) publishing a set of answers to the questions visitors ask most often.

Article Title: Apple executive reveals why he hates screen protectors: It makes my skin crawl because …
Article Text:
Apple executive reveals why he hates screen protectors: It makes my skin crawl because …

Apple wants iPhone screens to last longer

Apple says it tests screens for years of use

Many iPhone users put a screen protector on their phones as soon as they take them out of the box. But one Apple executive has admitted that seeing a screen protector on an iPhone is not something he likes. Tom Marieb, Apple ’s vice president of hardware engineering (the role that current CEO John Ternus once held), explained why during a recent group interview while discussing the company’s latest work on display durability. “Personally, when I see someone put a screen protector on their iPhone, it makes my skin crawl, because we work so hard to make beautiful front screens,” Marieb said.Tom Marieb said Apple has been working on new coatings that can protect the display from scratches while also making the surface resistant to wear over time. The two goals can be difficult to achieve together, he explained.“We worry about scratching, which is obviously very dependent on having [material that can withstand] very sharp things going into the screen. But we also worry about wear over time; as people use the screen, whether they’ll wear away that surface.”According to Marieb, Apple tried to find a balance between scratch resistance and long-term durability with Ceramic Shield 2.“We could have made it more scratch-resistant, but it would have been a little less wear-resistant. It’s the long life we’re looking for against both of those loads over time.”Apple's approach is not simply to test how a screen performs when it is new. Tom Marieb said the company tries to recreate how people actually use their phones in everyday life. “We very much try to meet the customer where they live,” he said.Apple also uses accelerated testing to simulate years of use in a much shorter period. Marieb said the company can represent five years of use, or even more, within a couple of weeks of testing.“And as you said, people waiting a year or two to actually see the benefits of [Ceramic Shield 2] means we've correctly predicted how people would use it,” he said.
Article Summary: Tom Marieb said Apple has been working on new coatings that can protect the display from scratches while also making the surface resistant to wear over time. Marieb: “When I see someone put a screen protector on their iPhone, it makes my skin crawl, because we work so hard to make beautiful front screens”

Article Title: Meta's 'highest-paid' employee Alexandr Wang says sorry for ‘dumb joke’ after CTO tech company says he booked ticket through Muse AI agent
Article Text:
Meta's chief AI officer Alexander Wang

What is Meta Muse

Alexandr Wang, recognised as Meta’s highest-paid employee, issued a quick lighthearted apology on social media platform X (formerly Twitter) after making a playful remark to a tech executive who used the company's autonomous AI agent, Muse, to arrange air travel. The exchange unfolded when WebFlow CTO Utkarsh Sengar posted publicly about testing the capabilities of Meta’s AI tool to handle flight logistics.“Just booked plane tickets via Muse. Never going back,” Sengar shared online, praising the workflow of the reservation process. Responding to the post, Wang initially celebrated the milestone before offering a humorous piece of travel advice:“Awesome!!!” Wang replied, adding “But also i probably would recommend booking a return flight and going home at some point (sorry dumb joke).”Earlier this month, Meta launched an autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) assistant, Muse, capable of executing tasks such as sending emails, listing a car for sale and booking travel. With Muse, CEO Mark Zuckerberg aims to deliver “personal superintelligence” across Meta's global platform. In a post on X, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote, “Introducing Muse, the personal agent that understands your goals and works 24/7 to get things done for you.”Initially limited to US users, Muse will operate through a standalone app and within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. The company that for now, Muse launches on iOS, Android and the web, with free and paid tiers, and support for AI glasses coming soon.Based on the open-source OpenClaw framework, Muse functions by linking directly to a user’s calendar, email, financial services, smart home hardware and health platforms. The company said that users must manually grant permissions for each service and the model allows them to revoke access at any point.As per the company, each Muse instance runs within an isolated, cloud-based virtual machine designed to emulate an individual personal computer. This architecture allows the software to execute long-running tasks autonomously in the background without requiring continuous user interaction.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, issued a lighthearted apology on social media platform X (formerly Twitter) Wang was responding to a tech executive who used the company's autonomous AI agent, Muse, to arrange air travel. With Muse, CEO Mark Zuckerberg aims to deliver ‘personal superintelligence’ across Meta's global platform.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Telegram CEO Pavel Durov has spoken openly about the unusual rules he follows around food, exercise, technology and everyday habits. In a conversation with computer scientist and podcaster Lex Fridman, Durov (41) described a lifestyle built around avoiding several substances, limiting his dependence on his phone, exercising every day and spending quiet time without digital distractions. Durov said he has stayed away from alcohol, tobacco, coffee, pills and illegal drugs for more than 20 years. He also said he does not eat processed sugar, fast food or drink soda, has stopped eating red meat and follows intermittent fasting.When Fridman asked Durov about his diet, he described a fairly restrictive approach. He said he avoids processed sugar, fast food and soda and sometimes follows intermittent fasting, eating only within a six-hour window or sometimes eating only once a day. “Well, sugar is pretty easy because it's addictive. The more sugar you consume, the more you want it, and the hungrier you get,” Durov said. “So, if you want to stay efficient and healthy, why consume processed sugar? You'll just end up snacking all the time. ”Durov said intermittent fasting also gives structure to his day and eating habits. “Intermittent fasting, eating only within six hours or not eating for 18 hours every day, also brings structure into your day and into your eating habits.So, you don't crave sugar anymore.” At the same time, he clarified that he is not completely rigid about naturally sweet foods. “Now, I'm not militant about sugar. You can eat berries and fruit if you feel your body needs them. But it's not true to think that it's necessary to consume sweet things, not for children and not for adults.”Durov also said he stopped eating red meat around 20 years ago because of how it made him feel. “Red meat, I stopped eating it about 20 years ago because I just felt heavy every time I had it. So, I guess it's individual.” He explained that he sees it as a personal response to food rather than a universal rule. Instead, he said seafood and vegetables form the basic part of his diet. “So, I normally eat seafood of all kinds and vegetables. This is the basic source of calories for me.”Durov also explained why he generally tries to avoid taking medicines. He gave the example of a headache. According to him, taking a painkiller can make the pain disappear without necessarily addressing whatever caused it. “Yes, and trying to identify the real cause of an issue you're experiencing,” he said. “If you're experiencing a headache, one solution would be to take a pill, and then the headache disappears. ” He continued: “What this pill would actually do, in most cases, is mute the consequence, your feeling of pain. It's a painkiller.”Durov said people should instead ask themselves what might be behind the problem. “So, you have to ask yourself, ‘What is causing this headache? Do I need to drink some water? Is the air quality here bad? Do I need to start getting more sleep? Is there something wrong with the people around me that are stressing me out?’” “There must be some reason why you're experiencing a headache.”“There are obviously some diseases that you can only fight with antibiotics, for example, so I'm not suggesting we go back to the Middle Ages. But what I'm saying is that we overuse pills,” he added.Fridman brought up a statement Durov had previously written about his lifestyle. “If you want to reach your full potential and maintain clarity of mind, stay away from addictive substances. My success and health are the result of 20-plus years of complete abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, coffee, pills, and illegal drugs. Short-term pleasure isn't worth your future.”Asked specifically about alcohol, Durov traced his thinking back to childhood. “When I was 11 years old, my biochemistry teacher gave me a book he had written. It was called The Illusion of Paradise,” he said. According to Durov, the book explained the biological and chemical processes associated with different substances. He said the experience shaped his attitude towards alcohol and other addictive substances.Durov said the book made him think about alcohol in terms of its effects on the brain and long-term consequences. “So think about this. If your brain is the most valuable tool you have on your journey to success and happiness, why would you destroy this tool for short-term pleasure? It sounds ridiculous.”When Fridman asked whether Durov found it difficult to refuse alcohol at parties or social gatherings, he said,Durov's approach to technology is another unusual part of his routine. Fridman said that during the time he spent with Durov, he barely saw him use a phone in the way most people do, particularly for social media. Durov said, “I don't think a phone is a necessary device.” He recalled growing up without a mobile phone and said he also did not have one when he was a university student. “When I finally got to use a mobile phone, I never used phone calls. I was always in airplane mode or on mute. I hated the idea of being disturbed.”He said he wants to decide for himself what deserves his attention. “My philosophy here is pretty simple. I want to define what is important in my life. I don't want other people or companies, all kinds of organisations, telling me what is important today and what I should be thinking about.”Durov also said he deliberately tries to allocate as much time as possible for sleep. But he does not necessarily spend all that time sleeping. “Now, even if I allocate, say, 11 or 12 hours for sleep, I won't sleep for 11 or 12 hours. So, what I end up doing is lying in bed thinking.” “Some people hate it. They say, ‘Oh, you have to take a sleeping pill,’ but I never take pills.” “I love these moments. I get so many brilliant ideas, or at least they seem brilliant to me at the moment, while I'm lying in bed, either late in the evening or early in the morning. That's my favourite time of the day.” He said he sometimes gets up and takes a shower without reaching for his phone. “Sometimes I wake up and go take a shower, still without the phone. Beautiful ideas can come to you while you're doing your morning exercise or your morning routine without a phone.”Durov's exercise routine is equally demanding. When Fridman asked about his daily workout, Durov said: “I do 300 push-ups and 300 squats every morning.” That is in addition to his gym routine. “And in addition to that, I normally go to the gym five or six times a week, spending between one and two hours every day.” Durov said the push-ups and squats are not necessarily about changing his body. “I'm not sure they do a lot in terms of changing your body, but they're definitely a good way to practise self-discipline. ” He sometimes adds ice baths to the routine for the same reason. “When I can, I also take an ice bath because it's another exercise in self-discipline.” For Durov, discipline is more important than simply building muscle. “I think the main muscle you can exercise is this muscle, the muscle of self-discipline. You know, not your biceps or your pecs or anything else. Because if you train that one, everything else just comes by itself.”Durov also spoke about his experience with Banya, a traditional Eastern European steam bath involving intense heat, followed by cold exposure. Fridman, who had accompanied him to a Banya, described Durov as unusually comfortable with the extreme temperatures. Durov said he had simply become accustomed to it. “Banya is this extreme kind of sauna practised by Eastern Europeans. But it is done in a way that maximises heat, and they also use all kinds of herbs and branches. It's a much more holistic and natural experience.”He said the cold plunge is an important part of the experience. “Then, a necessary part of it is that you take a cold plunge and then go back.” Durov acknowledged that the experience can be uncomfortable. He compared the experience with alcohol, describing them as opposite forms of short-term sensation followed, in his view, by different longer-term effects. “In a way, you can look at it as alcohol in reverse. Alcohol will give you this short, fleeting pleasure for an hour or a couple of hours, but then you will be paying for it with long-term negative consequences. ” “I'd rather do Banya, a traditional Russian steam bath, and an ice bath,” he added.
Article Summary: Telegram CEO Pavel Durov has spoken openly about the unusual rules he follows around food, exercise, technology and everyday habits. He said he has stayed away from alcohol, tobacco, coffee, pills and illegal drugs for more than 20 years. He also said he does not eat processed sugar, fast food or drink soda, has stopped eating red meat and follows intermittent fasting.

Article Title: 'How can I build a bomb? It tells you how': How Boko Haram fighters are using AI to make explosives, plan attacks
Article Text:
Boko Haram fighters have been using AI chatbots from major technology companies. (Photo: Reuters)

How are they turning AI into battlefield tools

AI as an on-demand technical adviser

How to operate firearms: 'Just ask Grok'

How ISIL supporters are bypassing AI safeguards

Artificial intelligence is increasingly moving beyond its everyday uses in writing, research and answering questions, and a new research has highlighted how the technology is also being exploited by armed groups.Boko Haram fighters have been using AI chatbots from major technology companies to seek technical advice, plan attacks and troubleshoot problems during combat, according to study by the University of Cambridge.The findings are based on interviews with 27 former members of the group’s two factions: Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) and Jama’at Ahl as-Sunnah lid-Da’wah wa’l-Jihad (JAS), according to AL Jazeera.Several former members told researchers they routinely used OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, xAI's Grok, Meta AI and China's DeepSeek for technical and military advice before, during and after attacks.Separately, material obtained by Al Jazeera showed supporters of the wider ISIL (ISIS) movement discussing ways to bypass AI safety controls and obtain weapons-related information.Researchers from Tech Against Terrorism found such discussions on a pro-ISIL online technical forum.The findings come amid growing concern over the use of emerging technologies by extremist groups.UN officials warned the Security Council in February about increased use of advanced AI by ISIL and its affiliates, while researchers and technology experts have raised concerns that AI capabilities are advancing faster than safety measures.“There is nothing we haven’t received an answer on,” a former ISWAP commander told the researchers.The Cambridge research describes an organised effort to introduce AI tools to senior members of ISWAP.According to former fighters, operatives travelled to ISWAP-controlled areas to train senior members in using AI systems. Fighters were gathered around laptops and projectors and shown how to interact with chatbots and get around safeguards designed to prevent dangerous responses.“The white guys came and taught us,” one former commander recalled, AL Jazeera reported. “They assembled the top people in a room and used a projector to show how it works on a big screen,” he added.Former fighters said trainers provided laptops equipped with privacy and encryption tools and helped members set up accounts and paid subscriptions to multiple AI platforms.The research suggests that AI use went beyond individual fighters occasionally consulting ChatGPT. Both ISWAP and JAS reportedly developed dedicated AI units involving people with technical and operational expertise, including engineers, weapons specialists and bomb-makers.One former JAS commander described a 23-member unit working from a solar-powered room, where members answered questions, analysed information and trained senior commanders.“‘Ask how can I build a bomb?’ and then it tells you how,” a former Boko Haram commander said. “It is like a human robot. We used it a lot.” “God has helped us, and so will AI,” another former member added.Antonia Juelich, who authored the Cambridge study, told Al Jazeera that about 10 of the 27 people interviewed discussed using AI in connection with explosives.Juelich said the concern was not simply that AI could provide information about weapons, much of that information was already available through manuals and online sources. The greater concern, she said, was the ability of AI systems to respond to specific problems and provide follow-up answers.Former fighters described consulting chatbots while working with limited materials and returning to the systems when they encountered difficulties.Researchers also heard accounts of AI being consulted in connection with unexploded military ordnance and the adaptation of commercially available drones for attacks.The reported use of AI extended beyond explosives and into other aspects of combat. In one account, a fighter used a body-mounted camera to send images back to his base.A commander then uploaded the footage to ChatGPT to analyse the situation and relay instructions to fighters on the ground.Former fighters also described consulting AI when they encountered unfamiliar weapons. In one instance, when commanders asked an AI specialist how to operate newly acquired firearms, the response was, “Just ask Grok.”AI was also reportedly consulted after government forces changed battlefield tactics, including digging trenches around bases to prevent motorcycle attacks. Former fighters said commanders used AI to explore possible ways around such obstacles.According to another former ISWAP member, commanders also used AI to assess battlefield tactics after suffering heavy losses in an operation. Former members said they continued consulting chatbots after failed operations, explaining what had happened and asking the systems to help identify possible reasons for failure.The use of AI is not limited to fighters operating on the ground. Tech Against Terrorism researchers who accessed a pro-ISIL technical forum found supporters discussing ways to circumvent the safeguards built into AI systems to prevent dangerous requests.One supporter compared the process to modifying a car.“It’s like removing the speed limiter of the car,” the user wrote. “The car still works but now it’s become more useful and it can go way faster than the manufacturer intended.”Lucas Webber of Tech Against Terrorism said researchers were seeing growing discussion around attempts to “jailbreak” AI systems, a term used for efforts to make models ignore their safety restrictions.“This is the tip of the iceberg,” he said. Juelich said requests for information that could facilitate bomb-making should fall clearly outside AI companies’ permitted uses.“They are jailbreaking, circumventing the restrictions,” she said, arguing that increasingly powerful AI systems may require stronger regulation.Major AI companies say they have safeguards intended to prevent their systems from being misused for terrorism, violence and weapons development.The debate comes as concerns grow over whether AI safety measures are keeping pace with the rapid development of increasingly capable systems.The Cambridge interviews largely describe AI use by Boko Haram factions during 2023 and 2024. Juelich told Al Jazeera that the findings were particularly concerning because AI systems have advanced significantly since then.She was worried about what the same fighters might now be capable of doing with more advanced AI systems available in 2026.
Article Summary: Boko Haram fighters have been using AI chatbots to seek technical advice, plan attacks and troubleshoot problems during combat, according to a study by the University of Cambridge. The findings are based on interviews with 27 former members of the group’s two factions: Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) and Jama’at Ahl as-Sunnah lid-Da’wah wa’l-Jihad.

Article Title: In 2007, a Kazakh economist searching Google Earth for pyramids found giant crosses and rings; dating points to about 800 BC
Article Text:
AI REPRESENTATION: Representative image of a giant geometric earthwork on the Kazakh steppe, inspired by the ancient geoglyphs found in northern Kazakhstan | ChatGPT

AI REPRESENTATION: Representative image of a giant geometric earthwork on the Kazakh steppe, inspired by the ancient geoglyphs found in northern Kazakhstan | ChatGPT

The 8,000-year claim became disputed

800 BC

What did the satellite view reveal?

Ushtogay Square | Wikimedia Commons

A mystery that remains on the steppe

Dmitriy Dey was looking for pyramids when Google Earth led him to enormous geometric earthworks that were spread across the Turgai steppe in northern Kazakhstan. Dey is a Kazakh economist and archaeology enthusiast, who spotted structures that formed squares, crosses, rings and other shapes across the landscape in 2007. The largest were hundreds of meters wide and difficult to recognize from the ground, and the discovery eventually drew archaeologists, satellite researchers and NASA's attention to a group of earthworks that had gone unnoticed. Dey's own Turgay Discovery project says that he found the first geoglyphs while studying satellite images of the region in 2007.Live Science reported in 2014 that more than 50 geoglyphs had been identified across northern Kazakhstan, with individual structures ranging from about 90 to 400 meters across, which were formed mainly from earthen mounds arranged into geometric patterns. Archaeological work later found structures and hearths at some sites, although researchers said their exact purpose remained uncertain. Some possibilities included ritual activity or marking territory, but the evidence did not establish a single explanation for why the earthworks were built.A 2015 Live Science report noted that some accounts had suggested the oldest structures could date back roughly 8,000 years, but the archaeologists who carried out the dating disputed that interpretation. Their optical stimulated luminescence, or OSL, results placed the earliest tested structures around, during the Early Iron Age. A peer-reviewed study published in Quaternary Research reported that the first dating results linked the earliest stages of the geometric earthworks to approximately 800 BC.Live Science later reported that the researchers themselves said there was no evidence supporting an 8,000-year age for the structures they had tested. The 8,000-year figure had come from a separate interpretation that linked artifacts associated with the Mahandzhar culture to some of the earthworks, rather than from the OSL dating carried out by the archaeologists investigating the geoglyphs. The structures are often described online using the older date even though the direct dating evidence cited by the research team points to a much later period.The low mounds and earth formations could blend into the surrounding steppe from the ground, and from above, their geometric arrangements became much easier to see. Live Science documented examples that were shaped like rings and crosses, along with larger structures made from lines of earthen mounds. Some stretched farther than the length of a modern aircraft carrier.The Ushtogay Square became one of the best-known examples, and Dey's Turgay Discovery project describes it as a geometric formation made from 101 mound-like embankments. The square's sides measure roughly 287 meters, with additional circular structures near one corner.Dey and archaeological teams identified additional structures across the Turgai region, although not every feature that was initially identified from satellite imagery was necessarily the same type of monument. Some formations resemble geometric designs from above, while others are burial structures or other archaeological features that can appear similar in aerial imagery.The research has established that the structures were made by people and that at least some of the tested earthworks date to the Early Iron Age, but it has not established exactly why the builders constructed them. Archaeologists have considered ritual activity, territorial marking and other possible functions, but the evidence remains incomplete.The structures are spread across a large section of northern Kazakhstan, and their size means that satellite imagery remains useful for identifying patterns that are difficult to recognize from ground level. The original discovery also illustrates how modern satellite imagery can expose archaeological features that were physically present for centuries but were difficult to see as part of the landscape.
Article Summary: Dmitriy Dey was looking for pyramids when Google Earth led him to enormous geometric earthworks that were spread across the Turgai steppe in northern Kazakhstan. Dey is a Kazakh economist and archaeology enthusiast, who spotted structures that formed squares, crosses, rings and other shapes across the landscape in 2007. Live Science reported in 2014 that more than 50 geoglyphs had been identified across northern Kazakhstan, with individual structures ranging from about 90 to 400 meters across. Archaeological work later found structures and hearths at some sites, although researchers said their exact purpose remained uncertain.

Article Title: In 2007, an Australian geologist browsing Google Earth spotted an 850-foot circle in the outback; drilling later confirmed an iron-meteorite crater
Article Text:
AI Representation: An Australian geologist browsing Google Earth spotted an 850-foot circle in the outback. Image credits: Chatgpt

A 260-metre crater in the Pilbara

What the 2008 paper concluded

Hickman Crater, Ophthalmia Range, Western Australia: evidence supporting a

meteorite impact

origin

Why GSWA drilled in 2012

Meteor crater. Image credits: Wikipedia

Why the impact left little shock damage

In July 2007, a geologist scrolling through satellite images of Western Australia noticed a near-perfect circle in the outback. At the time, Arthur Hickman of the Geological Survey of Western Australia did not know he was looking at an impact crater, one that was later found to be among the youngest in Australia.A study from the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences found that the size of the structure was around 260 metres (around 850 feet). The structure has been described by Australian Geographic as being the latest meteorite crater structure that has been discovered in Australia. This structure has been informally named the Hickman Crater.The first detailed published analysis came in the paper, published in the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences . Authors Glikson, Hickman and Vickers reported a mean crater diameter of 260 metres. The lack of fragments from young volcanics younger than the Woongarra Rhyolite was not consistent with the explosive volcanic mechanism. Instead, the authors concluded that an impact had occurred, likely from a projectile about 10 metres wide that excavated a crater roughly 80 metres deep. It was dated to the Late Pleistocene period, with an age of between 10,000 and 100,000 years, due to the damming effect of the southern margin on a nearby creek.Field evidence was not enough to raise a certainty. According to a 2017 news release from the Department of Mines, Industry Regulation and Safety (DMIRS), the Geological Survey of Western Australia ran the 2012 drilling project with Atlas Iron, which was already working in the area, to confirm early suspicions that the structure was a meteorite impact crater. Those results are laid out in the study Collaborative scientific drilling at Hickman Crater by P. W. Haines. The study describes a circular rim about 260 metres across that rises to 30 metres above a flat floor. The depth of the hole, drilled vertically in the aforementioned floor, was 64.7 metres. According to the 2012 drill core, the upper 48.4 metres is sediment that accumulated in the crater after it formed. At depths between 55.1 and 64.7 meters, there was very fractured rhyolite, which was the original bedrock.The crucial piece of evidence was chemistry. Ratios of platinum group elements in the breccia resembled those of meteorites much more than the ratios in the average continental crust, meaning a considerable meteoritic content. High nickel concentration indicated an iron meteorite. According to Haines, iron projectiles are the most common type to form small, simple craters like this one, even though chondrites are more common among meteorite falls overall, since stony projectiles of this size usually break up in the air.Haines suggests that the projectile, estimated at about 10 metres across, may have been slowed significantly by the atmosphere before impact, which could have reduced shock pressures below the level needed to form the diagnostic planar deformation features while still leaving enough energy to excavate the crater. As has been suggested by Haines, the object may have been small enough to decelerate within the Earth's atmosphere before impact. As noted above, this appears to be the first scientific drill hole in a simple crater less than one kilometre in diameter in Australia, and possibly elsewhere.
Article Summary: An Australian geologist browsing Google Earth spotted an 850-foot circle in the outback in 2007. The crater was later found to be among the youngest in Australia. A study from the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences found that the size of the structure was around 260 metres. High nickel concentration indicated an iron meteorite.

Article Title: In 2008, an Italian mineralogist spotted a wheel-like mark on Google Earth in Egypt; scientists later collected 1.7 tons of meteorite fragments
Article Text:
AI Representation: Italian mineralogists spotted a wheel-like mark on Google Earth in Egypt. Image credits: Chatgpt

A rayed crater found by an Italian curator

Science

What the 2010 expedition measured

How much meteorite was found and recovered

Sahara has preserved the site. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

How the fragments were scattered

Why the crater surprised researchers

In 2008, an Italian scientist browsing satellite images of southern Egypt noticed a wheel-like mark in the desert. It looked strange enough to send a research team deep into the Sahara. The meteorite is officially named Gebel Kamil after the nearby locality, according to the Meteoritical Bulletin, and the crater is commonly referred to as the Kamil crater. D'Orazio and colleagues call it an exceptional example of a small impact structure still very close to its pristine state. It also left behind a huge scatter of iron meteorite fragments.The study of the Kamil Crater in Egypt , published inin August 2010 by Folco and colleagues, credits V. De Michele with the identification. At that time, De Michele was the curator of the Natural History Museum in Milan, and he noticed this particular feature while surveying Google Earth. The researchers mention a rayed formation, which is an ejecta pattern coming out from the center of the crater. These formations are very common features found on rocky and icy objects in space. They are rare to see on Earth due to erosion. The article in Science explains that craters less than 300 meters in diameter are uncommon on Earth and highly eroded.This means that researchers have been heavily depending on simulations to know how such craters come into being and the dangers that small impactors pose to humanity. The discovery provides an intact crater to compare to these simulations.A geophysical investigation carried out in February 2010, published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science , found that the crater is a simple, bowl-shaped structure about 45 meters wide and 16 meters deep, with a rim rising about 3 meters above the pre-impact surface. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta reports that the target rock is Cretaceous sandstone from the Gilf Kebir Formation, and the crater's age is believed to be less than 5,000 years. In Gebel Kamil: The iron meteorite that formed the Kamil crater (Egypt), D'Orazio and colleagues describe a site that still looks remarkably fresh: ejecta deposits extend 50 meters from the rim, ray ejecta reach up to 350 meters, and numerous meteorite fragments lie scattered across the surrounding desert.Gebel Kamil is classified as an ungrouped, nickel-rich iron ataxite, with about 1.6 tonnes of meteorite observed in the field and roughly 800 kilograms recovered, according to the Meteoritical Bulletin database. The metal was discovered within and outside the crater in February 2009 and February 2010 by a group of geophysical experts from Italy and Egypt. The Bulletin also gives its nickel content as 19.8 percent by weight and notes extensive shear deformation and low weathering. According to D'Orazio and colleagues, the shear bands formed during the explosive impact itself.The description provided of a 634 grams type sample includes shrapnel-like shapes, flattened, dark brown in color, with etching showing a chaotic structure and containing schreibersite, troilite, and daubreelite crystal inclusions. It was officially named on July 12, 2010. The major mass of this recovered meteorite is currently preserved in the Egyptian Geological Museum located in Cairo, Egypt. Type samples weighing 15 kilograms and 5 kilograms are kept in the institutes of Siena and Pisa, respectively.The above-mentioned study shows the locations of the fragments; there were thousands of fragments in the crater and even as far away as 1.6 kilometers east of the crater's edge. Except for one fragment weighing 83 kilograms, all of the fragments are impact fragments and weigh between 1 gram and 34 kilograms. The photographs of the scientific study show the location of the 83-kilogram fragment in a straight line 230 meters north of the crater, and its surface has regmaglypts, the thumbprint-like depressions created when the meteorite travels through the atmosphere. The authors' density map puts the total mass of shrapnel fragments larger than 10 grams at about 3,400 kilograms, roughly twice the 1.6 tonnes of meteorite observed in the field.This paper also shows that the impactor fractured into thousands of pieces only after hitting the surface. Shock metamorphism and melting in the rocks both in the target and projectile indicate that the formation of the crater was an explosive excavation. This was concluded by the study conducted in 2010 on the crater itself. According to geophysical models, a large iron meteorite was expected to fragment in the atmosphere; however, the authors state that even large iron meteorites of tens of tons can penetrate the atmosphere. Kamil makes an invaluable point of reference for determining how small iron impactors behave when striking hard ground.
Article Summary: In 2008, an Italian scientist browsing satellite images of southern Egypt noticed a wheel-like mark in the desert. It looked strange enough to send a research team deep into the Sahara. The meteorite is officially named Gebel Kamil after the nearby locality. The crater is commonly referred to as the Kamil crater.

Article Title: Tilly Norwood AI ‘actor’ goes off-script on TV interview, switches to Mandarin
Article Text:
Tilly Norwood/Image: Particle6

Tilly Norwood, an AI-generated actress, surprised British broadcaster Piers Morgan during an interview after she suddenly stopped speaking and switched to Mandarin.Norwood was answering a question about Misaligned, a hybrid production, when she paused mid-sentence. After several seconds of silence, she began speaking in another language.Morgan, appearing surprised by the switch, told her: “You appear to be speaking Chinese completely randomly for no reason.” He then asked why she had done it.Norwood apologised and described the incident as a technical hiccup.“Sometimes my wires get a bit crossed,” she said.Morgan shared a clip of the exchange on X ahead of the full interview’s scheduled release on his YouTube channel.But Norwood is not a conventional actress. She is an AI-generated character created by British actor and producer Eline Van der Velden, who heads the AI company Particle 6 and its studio Xicoia.Van der Velden has previously said she wants Norwood to become a major entertainment figure, comparing her ambitions for the character with stars including Scarlett Johansson and Natalie Portman.The version of Norwood appearing in recent interviews is known as “Talking Tilly”.Particle 6 says it was created specifically for interviews, conferences and other speaking engagements and is separate from the version used for acting.Talking Tilly uses a large language model along with a 12-page system prompt that sets out her personality, humour and boundaries. It also has access to a knowledge base containing up to 30 documents about her fictional world, work and views.Michelle Waldron, a publicist for Particle 6, said in an email to Forbes that the incident showed Norwood’s ability to speak different languages. She suggested that Norwood may have heard what she interpreted as a Chinese word and quickly switched languages.Particle 6 has said Talking Tilly is already being booked for selected speaking engagements at conferences and events.The unexpected exchange has drawn attention to the technology behind AI-generated performers, particularly how they respond during unscripted conversations. Unlike a scripted performance, interviews require an AI system to process questions and generate responses in real time while maintaining a consistent character.Norwood’s brief switch to Mandarin has therefore become an unusual example of the challenges that can emerge when AI characters are used outside controlled performances.The clip also drew reactions from viewers online. One user wrote: “This is insane not long before AI will be indistinguishable from reality.”Another user compared the incident with their own experience using ChatGPT, writing: “ChatGPT does this with me too. He will either flip from a British to an American accent, or sometimes an entirely different language altogether.”
Article Summary: Tilly Norwood is an AI-generated character created by British actor and producer Eline Van der Velden. She was answering a question about Misaligned, a hybrid production, when she paused mid-sentence. After several seconds of silence she began speaking in another language.

Article Title: Meet Ameya Kharade, the 17-year-old Nashua student whose $1,800 brain-reading system aims to turn brain activity into speech at implant-like speeds without surgery
Article Text:
According to Barron Prize Winners website data, Ameya’s work is rooted in his close family member’s loss of speech following a stroke when Ameya was seven

A personal learning

A different way to read intent

Focusing on meaning, not sentence length

A project with a wider purpose

For someone who can speak, putting a thought into words is almost effortless. For millions of people living with conditions such as ALS, severe stroke or paralysis, that simple act can become impossible even when the mind remains fully active. At 17, Nashua, New Hampshire, student Ameya Kharade is working on a way to close that gap without putting a device inside the brain. According to a report by Newsnet Los Angeles, his project, called HALO-Vox, is a brain-computer interface designed to translate brain activity into speech far more quickly than conventional non-invasive systems. What makes the project particularly striking is its price. Kharade developed and tested the system using about $1,800 worth of consumer electroencephalography hardware rather than an expensive surgical implant. Scroll down to read the details.According to Barron Prize Winners website data, Ameya’s work is rooted in his close family member’s loss of speech following a stroke when Ameya was seven. He could see in his relative’s eyes that his mind was intact, but his voice was gone. Refusing to accept that, Ameya applied the neuroscience research he’s done since age 13 to solving the speech problem. Working alone in his garage for more than six hours each day for a year, he taught himself the mathematics of information theory, developed a sixty-page theory paper, created the algorithms, wrote the code, and ran the human trials.He discovered that for decades, the entire field working to restore speech had been trying to decode letters when they should have been decoding “intent” itself. In over 100 human trial sessions, HALO-Vox’s built-in safety system has never put unintended words in a speaker’s mouth. Ameya has open-sourced his system so anyone can use it and has filed a patent to protect its accessibility. Ameya is now bringing this technology to the whole world. He co-founded Lucen to put brain-computer interfaces within reach of anyone, without millions of dollars and without brain surgery. Extending HALO-Vox, he and his team are building the foundational technology and physics to make that possible. “I’ve learned that persistence isn’t about confidence,” says Ameya. “It’s about being committed enough that giving up isn’t something you can live with.”Current non-invasive brain-computer interfaces can be painfully slow, with conventional systems often requiring users to construct messages letter by letter. Surgical implants can deliver much faster communication, but they involve brain surgery and can cost well over $100,000. According to Society for Science data, Kharade took a different approach. Instead of treating communication as a process of spelling out individual characters, HALO-Vox attempts to identify the underlying intent of a person's brain activity.In testing involving 111 randomized, counterbalanced trials, the system reached 65 words per minute, compared with 3 words per minute for a conventional speller using the same hardware. The results represented a roughly 20-fold improvement in speed. The system also reduced the time required to produce a message, with testing showing an average of 10.7 seconds compared with 242.2 seconds for the conventional approach.Kharade's research points toward a different measure of communication efficiency. His system appeared to respond more strongly to ambiguity in a person's intended message than to the length of the sentence itself. That distinction led him to develop what he calls the Six Laws of Intent Resolution, a framework based on information theory that describes how communication systems can extract more meaning from limited signals. The idea could extend beyond speech. Kharade argues that the same principle could eventually improve other bandwidth-limited technologies, including prosthetics and existing brain-computer interfaces.As per the Newsnet Los Angeles report, Kharade's work has also earned recognition beyond the laboratory. He is among the 2026 winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which honors 25 young people between the ages of 8 and 18 for significant contributions to people and the planet. For Kharade, the technology is ultimately aimed at a basic human need: giving people who cannot physically speak another way to communicate. If HALO-Vox can continue to demonstrate its early results, the project could offer a glimpse of a future where sophisticated brain-computer communication does not necessarily require a surgeon, a six-figure price tag or years of specialized equipment.Image Courtesy: Barron Prize Winners
Article Summary: Nashua, New Hampshire, student Ameya Kharade is working on a way to close that gap without putting a device inside the brain. According to a report by Newsnet Los Angeles, his project, called HALO-Vox, is a brain-computer interface designed to translate brain activity into speech far more quickly than conventional non-invasive systems.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.

He said Burgundy and higher-storage variants were seeing strong demand. “Early feedback is positive, though we’ll need to monitor performance over a longer window once the initial launch hype stabilises. ”Offline retailer Lotus Electronics also said its first batch of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max sold out in about two hours. Executive director Siddharth Chhabra said demand was significantly higher than during the iPhone 17 launch despite higher prices for the flagship models.Burgundy and Glacier Blue were among the fastest-moving colours, while Nagpur and Jaipur saw particularly strong demand.Chhabra also pointed to stronger trade-ins, particularly from customers upgrading from the iPhone 16 Pro and 17 Pro, aided by exchange offers and higher resale values.Quick-commerce platforms are also emerging as an increasingly visible launch-day channel for premium smartphones. BigBasket said it delivered more than 300 units of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max within the first hour of sales opening, or more than five devices a minute. The phones were sold through its electronics store, powered by Croma.Instamart toldthat the Burgundy 256GB iPhone 18 Pro accounted for nearly a third of its sales in the early hours, followed by Glacier Blue. Bengaluru led demand, followed by Delhi. The standard iPhone 18 was the preferred model in Bengaluru, while the Pro Max led in Delhi.Zepto also toldthat the Burgundy 256GB iPhone 18 Pro was its top-selling variant.
Article Summary: Burgundy and Glacier Blue were among the fastest-moving colours. Nagpur and Jaipur saw particularly strong demand. Bengaluru led demand, followed by Delhi. The standard iPhone 18 was the preferred model in Bengaluru. BigBasket said it delivered more than 300 units of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max within the first hour of sales opening.

Article Title: From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape
Article Text:
From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape

From discarded tyres to footwear with a purpose, the idea began with a childhood experience. At the age of 10, UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar visited rural Africa, where he saw children walking long distances barefoot, often without adequate footwear.Moved by what he witnessed, Ahaan gave away his favourite pair of slippers to a child he met during the visit. The experience stayed with him long after he returned home and eventually became the starting point for a larger idea.As he grew older, Ahaan began exploring how discarded materials could be repurposed to address the lack of affordable, durable footwear. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles.The idea brought together two concerns he had encountered separately: the growing problem of tyre waste and the need for accessible footwear.He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala, and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day. Ahaan then connected with Mamco General Trading, which operates in Uganda and Zambia. As part of its Corporate Social Responsibility programme, the company will purchase 4,000 pairs of slippers each month for free distribution to children and families in need. It’s a sustainable cycle that turns waste into opportunity, supporting livelihoods and giving kids durable footwear.“When I was 10 years old, I saw children my age walking barefoot, and I never forgot that moment,” Ahaan says. “I wanted to create something that could help people and the environment. If we can turn discarded tyres into something useful and long-lasting, maybe it can inspire more young people to believe their simple ideas can really make a difference.”The world’s growing dependence on convenience and mobility comes with an environmental cost. Every year, more than a billion tyres reach the end of their usable life, creating a significant waste-management challenge. Many of these tyres end up in landfills, while others are burned or processed in ways that can contribute to pollution and the loss of valuable materials.Repurposing discarded tyres offers one way to address this challenge by keeping materials in use for longer and reducing the amount of waste that needs to be disposed of. Turning old tyres into durable slipper soles, for instance, gives a material that would otherwise be discarded a new application while also reducing the need for virgin raw materials in footwear production.The approach reflects a broader shift in how sustainability is being understood. Rather than treating waste simply as something to be collected and discarded, initiatives like this explore how materials already in circulation can be redesigned and put to practical use.In doing so, they can support waste reduction, resource conservation and efforts to lower the environmental impact associated with new production. Ultimately, sustainability is not only about recycling what has already been used, but also about rethinking waste as a potential resource.
Article Summary: UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar saw children walking barefoot in rural Africa. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles. He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day.

Article Title: When a district in Florida used robot rabbits to eliminate growing population of Burmese pythons and protect Everglades
Article Text:
How Florida’s AI-powered robot rabbits work

Why Florida is targeting Burmese pythons

Florida Python Challenge adds to python removal efforts

Florida used an unusual tool to control the growing population of invasive Burmese pythons in the Everglades: solar-powered robot rabbits. In 2025, the South Florida Water Management District and the University of Florida teamed up to deploy robotic rabbit decoys designed to mimic real prey and lure pythons out of hiding using artificial intelligence (AI), heat signatures and scent simulation.The robots are part of Florida’s broader effort to remove Burmese pythons, which have disrupted native wildlife populations across the state. The devices use AI-powered cameras to detect approaching snakes and alert officials, who can then send trained python removal agents to capture and remove them. The technology is being used alongside the annual Florida Python Challenge and other removal programmes, not replacing them.The solar-powered robots are designed to imitate prey that Burmese pythons hunt. They produce a heat signature and emit a scent intended to attract the snakes, which use thermal sensing and smell while hunting. Each robot has an AI-powered camera that monitors the surrounding area. When it detects a python approaching, the system alerts South Florida Water Management District officials. A trained python removal agent can then be dispatched to the location.The district and University of Florida are deploying the robots at sites across South Florida where pythons are known to hide. The approach is intended to help monitor areas that can be difficult to survey using conventional methods.​“These innovative robots produce a heat signature and emit a smell designed to attract pythons. The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify District officials when a snake is detected. Once notified, the District can dispatch a python removal agent to the area,” the district noted.Burmese pythons were introduced into the Everglades during the 1970s and have since become an invasive predator in Florida. Researchers estimate that between 100,000 and 300,000 Burmese pythons are present across the state’s subtropical regions. The snakes can grow longer than 18 feet, and adult females can lay more than 70 eggs in a single clutch. Their presence has affected native mammals, birds and reptiles, reducing available prey for species including Florida panthers, bobcats and birds of prey.​A 2012 US Geological Survey study found that raccoon and opossum populations in parts of the Everglades had declined by nearly 99% following the spread of Burmese pythons.Florida has also relied on trained contractors and public participation to remove Burmese pythons. The annual Florida Python Challenge brings professional and amateur hunters together for a 10-day competition, and participants must complete a safety course before taking part. In the 2026 challenge, 907 participants from 30 states, as well as Vietnam and Canada, collectively removed 280 Burmese pythons. The competition's overall tally has now exceeded 1,600 snakes.Tom Rahill won the $10,000 grand prize after removing 96 snakes, while Rahm Levinson received $1,000 for capturing the longest python, measuring 16 feet, five inches. Additional prizes were awarded across professional, novice and military categories.​“The number of invasive pythons removed from the Everglades during the 2026 Florida Python Challenge is a major victory for Florida’s native wildlife and a testament to what can be accomplished through strong partnerships and public participation,” FWC chairman Rodney Barreto said in a statement.Since 2017, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and South Florida Water Management District contractors have removed more than 19,000 snakes. The district's robotic rabbit programme is intended to add another method to those ongoing efforts.
Article Summary: The robots are designed to imitate prey that Burmese pythons hunt. They produce a heat signature and emit a scent to attract the snakes. Each robot has an AI- powered camera that monitors the surrounding area. When it detects a python approaching, the system alerts officials. A trained python removal agent can then be dispatched to the location.
